meta.tagline: Where five-hundred-year-old palaces and neon streets live at once

overview.title: Welcome to Seoul
overview.intro: Seoul says speed and grace in the same sentence: a five-hundred-year-old ceremony is reenacted in the courtyard of Gyeongbokgung while, two streets over, a K-pop video breaks records over the world's fastest internet. The curve of hanok roofs and the gleam of glass towers share one frame; at midnight the street stalls still steam and the cafes stay open to dawn. Everything here runs 'ppalli ppalli' (quick, quick) — but the table culture refuses to hurry: time spent around the grill is Seoul's most precious hospitality.

local_word.definition: Korean's untranslatable word: the deep attachment and unconditional care woven over time. The stall keeper adding an extra piece to your plate, a host feeding you like their own child — all of it is jeong. Understanding Korea begins with noticing this invisible bond circulating at every table.

rules.title: Change your map: use Naver or Kakao
rules.description: Google Maps only half-works in Korea: download Naver Map or Kakao Map for walking and transit routes. Both have English interfaces and show metro exit numbers — in Seoul, a meeting place is given as 'station + exit number'.

rules.title: Learn the table manners: sharing is the rule
rules.description: The Korean table is built on shared plates: the banchan belong to everyone, and the grill is cooked together at the table. Don't leave your spoon standing in the rice bowl, and pause a beat before the eldest starts — small gestures earn great respect in this city.

rules.title: Tour the palace in hanbok, follow the palace rhythm
rules.description: Those wearing rented hanbok enter the palaces free: touring Gyeongbokgung in traditional dress is not a tourist gimmick — locals do it too. Time your visit to the changing of the guard — drums in the palace courtyard are the city's most graceful time travel.

quick_facts.label: Signature
quick_facts.sub: Palace and hanok village side by side

quick_facts.label: Currency
quick_facts.sub: A T-money card opens every gate

tip.label: The Seoul philosophy
tip.text: In this city you tour palaces by day and stalls by night: give half the program to history, half to neon. When tired, go to a jjimjilbang; when hungry, join a queue — in Seoul, the queue is quality's most honest advertisement.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: The Seoul metro is among the world's best: clean, punctual, English-friendly — with a T-money card the city fits in your palm.

items.title: Arriving from the airport
items.description: From Incheon, the AREX express reaches Seoul Station in 45 minutes; the all-stop AREX is slower but cheaper. For late-night landings, airport limousine buses fan out by district — taxis are comfortable but costly.

items.title: Metro mastery
items.description: Color-coded lines, numbered exits and English announcements: the metro is Seoul's spine. Buy a T-money card at any convenience store; transfers calculate automatically. Line 2 packs out at rush hour — wait one train, the next comes emptier.

items.title: Taxis and Kakao T
items.description: Taxis are reasonable by world standards: orange-and-silver is standard, black 'deluxe' is pricier. The Kakao T app ends the address problem — showing the driver an address in Korean is always the fastest solution.

items.title: Neighborhood walks
items.description: Seoul is walked neighborhood by neighborhood: Bukchon's slopes, Seongsu's warehouse lanes, Hongdae's young crowds. The Cheonggyecheon stream is a walking corridor through the city's middle — lovelier still under the night lights.

items.title: Night buses and mountain lines
items.description: The Owl buses run the main arteries after midnight; city buses reach the gates of Bukhansan and the other mountains. Few places escape the metro — the bus is its scenic complement.

callout.label: Metro tip
callout.text: Crack the address culture: 'Hongik Univ. Station, Exit 9' is an address. Type the station into Naver Map and follow the exit number — leaving by the wrong exit means an extra ten-minute walk in Seoul.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Seoul choosing a neighborhood means choosing a tempo: Myeongdong's practicality, Hongdae's night rhythm, Bukchon's hanok mornings.

local_word.definition: Underfloor heating: the thousand-year-old comfort system of the Korean home. In a traditional hanok you sleep on a floor mattress warmed from below — even modern apartments aren't built without ondol. When you feel the floor's warmth in a winter hanok stay, you've touched the heart of Korean home culture.

items.name: Myeongdong
items.description: The center of shopping streets, cosmetics shops and street-food stalls: strong metro links, everything within walking distance. The classic, painless base for a first visit.

items.name: Hongdae
items.description: The university quarter's street performances, clubs and cafes: alive late into the night. Direct to the airport on the AREX line — the address for young energy.

items.name: Bukchon and Insadong
items.description: The hanok village between the palaces and the art lanes beside it: tea houses, galleries, morning silence. An ondol experience with a hanok stay — for waking up inside history.

items.name: Gangnam
items.description: Broad boulevards, towers and polished restaurants: Seoul's glossy modern bank. COEX and Bongeunsa Temple sit side by side — the hub for business-and-comfort stays.

items.name: Seongsu
items.description: 'Seoul's Brooklyn', where old shoe factories became cafes and galleries: pop-up shops, third-wave coffee. Next to Seoul Forest park — for seeing the creative scene at the source.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Seoul lives its four seasons hard: cherry blossoms in spring, monsoon and festivals in summer, crimson leaves in autumn, freezing but ice-blue skies in winter.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The Cherry Blossom Wave
items.subtitle: Spring · Blossoming palace courtyards, riverside picnics
items.description: In early April the cherry blossoms sweep the city: Yeouido's tree tunnels, palace courtyards and campuses turn pink. The air warms and the Han River picnics begin — Seoul's most photogenic window.

callout.label: April tip
callout.text: Peak blossom lasts a week and the calendar shifts every year: follow the blossom forecast maps. Choose Seokchon Lake's morning hours over the Yeouido crowds — the same pink, a tenth of the people.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Monsoon and River Nights
items.subtitle: Summer · Humid heat, downpours, night picnics
items.description: July's monsoon arrives in downpours and August is humid and hot: days are built around air-conditioned museums and cafes, evenings around the Han River banks. The night picnic — a tent, fried chicken and a river breeze — is the signature of a Seoul summer.

callout.label: Monsoon note
callout.text: In mid-July, keep the umbrella in your bag: downpours strike suddenly — the umbrella-bagging machines at metro exits exist for a reason. The humidity wears you down; build one cafe-break layer into each day.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Crimson Leaf Peak
items.subtitle: Autumn · Clear skies, golden ginkgo avenues
items.description: October and November are Seoul at its best: crystal skies, cool air, ginkgo trees painting the avenues gold. Bukhansan's granite turns crimson and the palace courtyards catch their most graceful light — the season of walkers and photographers.

callout.label: November tip
callout.text: In early November the back garden of Gyeongbokgung and the Samcheong-dong road turn ginkgo-yellow: go early and walk while the light is low. It's also the year's best window for the Bukhansan summit hike — pick a weekday.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Ice-Blue Days
items.subtitle: Winter · Sub-zero cold, deep blue skies, steaming stalls
items.description: Seoul winter is fierce: minus ten happens, but the sky stays deep blue most days. The steam of street stalls, hotteok pancakes and jjimjilbang warmth are winter's rewards — and when snow falls, the palace courtyards become postcards.

callout.label: January tip
callout.text: On a freezing night, go to a jjimjilbang: hot pools, a salt room and a nap on the heated floor — Korean winter therapy. On the way out, buy a hot hotteok from a stall: the syrup filling burns your hand, and it's worth it.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: The Korean table is the architecture of sharing: meat over coals, an army of banchan in the middle, soju alongside — and everything has its etiquette.

local_word.definition: The army of small plates that arrives beside the main dish: kimchi, pickles, seasoned greens, tiny omelets. All included, all refillable — don't be surprised when the table fills with little plates; this is the constitution of the Korean table. Banchan generosity is the first sign of a good restaurant.

items.name: The samgyeopsal ritual
items.description: Pork belly or beef over coals set into your table: cut with scissors, wrapped in a lettuce leaf — garlic, ssamjang and a piece of kimchi inside. Eat the wrap in one bite; etiquette insists. The hour around the grill is the heart of Seoul's social life.
items.tag: Coals at the table · one-bite wraps

items.name: Gwangjang Market classics
items.description: At the century-old market's stalls: bindaetteok (mung-bean pancakes) and mayak gimbap ('addictive' mini rolls). Grab a stool and watch the aunties' mastery. The crowded stall is always the right stall.

items.name: Kimchi jjigae and a full table
items.description: Bubbling kimchi stew with rice and the banchan army: the cornerstone of Korean home cooking. A few dollars at a lunchtime eatery — its heat races its warmth, and the spoon is hard to put down.

items.name: Tteokbokki and the street stall
items.description: Rice cakes in sweet-hot sauce, with fish cakes and fried mandu alongside: the classic of the school run and the night walk. The pojangmacha (tent stall) atmosphere is half the experience — the steam is best in the cold.
items.tag: Street classic · at a tent stall

items.name: Chimaek: chicken + beer
items.description: Double-fried crisp Korean chicken with cold beer: the 'chikin + maekju' contraction is now an institution. Order half sauced, half plain, and eat it by the Han River — Seoul evening's most democratic pleasure.

items.name: Bingsu and cafe culture
items.description: Snow-fine shaved ice under sweet red bean, milk and fruit: bingsu is Seoul's sweet summit. The city's cafe scene is a reason to travel in itself — from theme cafes to rooftops, the coffee is taken seriously.
items.tag: Snow dessert · with the cafe scene

callout.label: Table rule
callout.text: Three signs of a good Seoul restaurant: a queue at the door, generous banchan on the table, few items on the menu. Grill houses sometimes require two portions for solo diners — then the stew and bibimbap eateries are your friends.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees Gyeongbokgung; these six are Seoul's hanok-scented, mountain-framed hidden face.

items.name: Ikseondong
items.description: Cafes, workshops and boutiques in the narrow lanes of restored hanoks: third-wave coffee under traditional roofs. Go on a weekday morning — the lanes fill by afternoon, but the morning is yours.

items.name: The Naksan fortress walls
items.description: The Naksan stretch of the city walls is lit at night: five-hundred-year-old stones on one side, a million-lighted city on the other. The route from Hyehwa down to Dongdaemun is Seoul's most romantic free activity.

items.name: Bukhansan National Park
items.description: Granite peaks rising out of the city: metro and bus deliver you to the gate, and within hours you're looking down on the megacity from bare rock. Few cities of millions have such a mountain this close — go on a weekday.

items.name: The jjimjilbang experience
items.description: Hot pools, salt and ice rooms, naps on heated floors and the sheep-head towel: the jjimjilbang is not a spa but a social institution. You can even stay the night — falling asleep on a warm floor is the Korean way of resetting.

items.name: Mangwon Market
items.description: A neighborhood market tourists rarely reach: fried-chicken stalls, home-style dishes and friendly prices. Shop, then walk five minutes to the Han River — market plus river picnic is the locals' weekend formula.

items.name: Seongsu and Seoul Forest
items.description: Old shoe factories became cafes, galleries and pop-up shops; next door, the deer groves of Seoul Forest. Split an afternoon between the two — Seoul's creative present and its green breath side by side.

callout.label: Tempo strategy
callout.text: Tour Seoul in layers: palace and hanok in the morning, a market stall at noon, a cafe or a mountain in the afternoon, a wall walk or neon street at night. When fatigue accumulates, the jjimjilbang resets you — this city runs fast, but it has institutionalized its breaks.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Seoul is honest and safe; its traps are small and easily dodged — keep these four in your pocket.

items.name: Trusting Google Maps
items.description: Map data is restricted in Korea: Google won't draw walking routes and its time estimates mislead — 'can't find the way' is the classic tourist problem in Seoul.
items.instead: Download Naver Map or Kakao Map and set them to English: metro exit numbers, bus times and walking routes work flawlessly. Copying addresses in Korean also saves lives in taxis.

items.name: The 'free gift' sales press in Myeongdong
items.description: In some cosmetics shops, the 'free mask' pressed on you at the door becomes a long, insistent sales chat inside; the basket swells and returns are hard.
items.instead: Decline the gift with a smile, or take it and skip the store if you need nothing. Shop at official single-brand stores and price-tagged chains — and carry your passport for tax-free shopping.

items.name: The late-night 'black taxi' haggle
items.description: Some drivers waiting in nightlife zones quote round numbers instead of the meter; tourists mistaking a deluxe cab for a standard one pay double.
items.instead: Call a ride with Kakao T or take a metered orange-and-silver taxi: the night surcharge is legal and modest, and haggling is unnecessary. Returning before the metro closes is always an option — check the last train.

items.name: Low-quality hanbok rentals
items.description: Some shops near the palaces rent the cheapest fabric at the highest price; 'mandatory extras' like hair accessories and bags inflate the bill.
items.instead: Ask clearly at the door what's included: hourly rate, accessories, hair? Choose a well-reviewed shop in advance — a quality hanbok shows its difference in the photos and in the palace.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: Getting lost in Seoul isn't dangerous, just time lost — with the right map, a T-money card and a few Korean words, the city works for you. When in doubt, ask the young: most treat helping in English as seriously as homework.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Itineraries
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. Times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From palace morning to neon night

steps.title: Gyeongbokgung and the guard ceremony
steps.description: Tour the palace courtyards in morning light and catch the changing of the guard. Rent a hanbok and entry is free — the photos last a lifetime.

steps.title: Bukchon and Ikseondong
steps.description: Roof curves on the hanok village slopes, then Ikseondong's cafe lanes: two hours where tradition and today shake hands.

steps.title: Gwangjang Market lunch
steps.description: Grab a stool for bindaetteok and mayak gimbap: the aunties' stall mastery is the show itself.

steps.title: Cheonggyecheon and Dongdaemun
steps.description: Walk the stream to the spaceship architecture of the DDP: Zaha Hadid's curves are at their best at sunset.

steps.title: The Naksan wall walk
steps.description: Climb to the walls from Hyehwa: as the lights come on, the city spreads at your feet. Seoul's most romantic free hour.

steps.title: Samgyeopsal and the night streets
steps.description: The wrap ritual around the coals, then Hongdae's street performances or a pojangmacha stall: the night doesn't end early in Seoul.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Palaces, a mountain and a river — the full Seoul

steps.title: Classic Seoul
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: the palace, Bukchon, Gwangjang, Cheonggyecheon, Naksan, a samgyeopsal night.

steps.title: Mountain or the modern bank
steps.description: By your energy: the Bukhansan summit hike in the morning, or Changdeokgung's Secret Garden (timed tour); Seongsu cafes and Seoul Forest in the afternoon; dinner in Gangnam + the book tower of the COEX library at night.

steps.title: River and farewell
steps.description: Morning picnic supplies from Mangwon Market, then bikes and grass along the Han River; Myeongdong shopping or a jjimjilbang break in the afternoon; farewell chimaek in the evening — closing with river breeze and crisp chicken.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Korean is a courteous language and effort is rewarded instantly; these five phrases open doors at the table and on the street.

items.meaning: Hello — with a slight bow; valid at every hour of the day
Thank you — from stall to metro, your most-used word
'I will eat well' — said before the meal; it wins the host's heart
Cheers! — as the soju rises; turning slightly away from elders while drinking is the custom
Please give me — combined with pointing, the key to the art of menu-free ordering
